content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the hierarchy of organisation in multicellular organisms
Define cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism
Give examples of each level of organisation in animals and plants
Explain how the levels of organisation are related

Multicellular organisms are highly organised. Cells don't just exist randomly - they are organised into increasingly complex structures that work together. This organisation follows a hierarchy, from the simplest level (cells) to the most complex (the whole organism).
Cells → Tissues → Organs → Organ Systems → Organism

attrs.alt: Pyramid showing levels of organisation from cells at the bottom to organism at the top

content.text: Each level is made up of the previous level working together:
The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.
Smallest unit that can carry out life processes
Examples: nerve cells, muscle cells, red blood cells, palisade cells
A group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function.
Supports, connects, or separates other tissues

attrs.alt: Different types of animal and plant tissues

content.text: A structure made of different tissues working together to perform a specific function.
Epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem

attrs.alt: Cross-section of a leaf showing different tissues forming the organ

content.text: A group of organs working together to perform a major function.
Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas
White blood cells, lymph nodes, spleen

attrs.alt: Overview of major human organ systems

content.text: A complete living thing made up of all organ systems working together.
Failure of one system affects others
Examples: humans, dogs, oak trees, bacteria (single-celled organism)
→ Stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas
Lower epidermis with stomata (gas exchange control)
Phloem sieve tubes and companion cells (sugar transport)

attrs.alt: Hierarchical breakdown of a leaf showing all levels

content.text: Understanding organ systems helps diagnose diseases
Organ transplants rely on understanding tissue compatibility
Tissue engineering aims to grow replacement organs
Understanding plant organ systems improves crop yields
Knowledge of root systems helps with irrigation
Understanding leaf structure helps optimise photosynthesis
Blood is a tissue (connective tissue). The circulatory system is an organ system
Skin is an organ - it's made of multiple tissues (epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous)
Single-celled organisms (like bacteria and some protists) are just one cell - they don't have tissues, organs, or organ systems
Plants do have organ systems - the root system and shoot system
Basic structural and functional unit of life
Group of similar cells performing a specific function
Structure made of different tissues working together
Group of organs working together for a major function
Tissue that covers surfaces and lines cavities
Tissue that supports, connects, or separates other tissues
Tissue that contracts to cause movement
Living organisms are organised in a hierarchy: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism
A tissue is a group of similar cells working together
An organ is made of different tissues working together
An organ system is a group of organs performing a major function
Both animals and plants show this hierarchical organisation
Understanding levels of organisation is essential for understanding how organisms function
